summary:
Erzincan province stands under the Turkish national legal framework. No Erzincan-specific ordinance, incident or court decision was found on record, so what a trans visitor faces in the province is determined by national law and national policing practice.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with the absence of any legal recognition for same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions or same-sex adoption, and with a bar on LGBTI people serving openly in the military.

Since 2015 the authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia. In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality".

Even a campus Pride march can draw criminal prosecution: ILGA-Europe urged Turkish courts on 7 December 2020 to acquit 19 human rights defenders prosecuted for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, calling on the state to uphold its domestic and international commitments and dismiss all charges. The national freedom-of-assembly climate and legal exposure of LGBT advocacy reflected in that case is the framework under which a visitor in Erzincan would be judged.
tangentialFactors: The national framework recorded under Turkey includes a draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague provisions protecting "the family" and "public morals"; whether it has since passed is unresolved in the sources. Erzincan-specific enforcement patterns are not documented, so the province's practical exposure cannot be distinguished from the national picture.
localsOnly: Residents of Erzincan live under the same national provisions as visitors: no legal recognition of same-sex relationships, no open military service for LGBTI people, and exposure to prosecution for participation in Pride-type events. No province-level discrimination complaint mechanism, local ordinance or regional protection body was identified in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes: Whether any Erzincan-specific enforcement incidents, local police practice or provincial court decisions concerning LGBT people exist is unresolved; the sources contain no province-level signal either way. The status of the reported early-2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality" is also unresolved in the sources.
